content: First-line therapy for tuberculous meningitis includes the following medications: 1. Isoniazid: Administered at a dose of 5 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 2 months during the intensive phase for adults. For pediatric patients, the dose is 10–15 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 2 months. 2. Rifampin: Administered at a dose of 10 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 2 months during the intensive phase for adults. For pediatric patients, the dose is 10–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 2 months. 3. Pyrazinamide: Administered at a dose of 15–30 mg/kg (maximum dose: 2 g) daily for 2 months during the intensive phase for both adults and pediatric patients. 4. Ethambutol: Administered at a dose of 15–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 1 g) daily for 2 months during the intensive phase for both adults and pediatric patients. The continuation phase for adults involves: Isoniazid: 5 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Rifampin: 10 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 7–10 months. The continuation phase for pediatric patients involves: Isoniazid: 10–15 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Rifampin: 10–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 7–10 months. For tuberculous meningitis caused by isoniazid-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Substitute a fluoroquinolone (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, or gatifloxacin) for isoniazid in the intensive phase regimen. Continue treatment with rifampin, pyrazinamide, and the fluoroquinolone for a total of 12 months. For tuberculous meningitis caused by rifampin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Substitute a fluoroquinolone for rifampin in the intensive phase regimen. Continue treatment with isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and the fluoroquinolone for a total of 18 months. For multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), defined as resistance to both isoniazid and rifampin: MDR-TB therapy should be considered in cases with a history of prior tuberculosis treatment, contact with a patient with MDR-TB, or poor clinical response to first-line therapy within 2 weeks despite confirmed diagnosis and adequate adherence to treatment. Second-line agents, such as aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin), may penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB) only in the presence of inflamed meninges. Fluoroquinolones can penetrate the central nervous system (CNS) but achieve lower cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels compared to serum or brain parenchyma. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is strongly recommended. For extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB), defined as resistance to isoniazid, rifampin, fluoroquinolones, and at least one of the injectable second-line agents (capreomycin, kanamycin, or amikacin): Consider using ethionamide or cycloserine to construct the treatment regimen. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is essential. These guidelines are based on recommendations from the American Thoracic Society, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the World Health Organization (WHO).
